# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# The strongest evidence in the set, with a few problems that matter

This follow-up answers the main open questions. The per-hour gain does decline, but it doesn't disappear. The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim rested on weak studies. Coverage-bound work was abandoned for cost reasons, which is the outcome Varden's nine-month results implied.

The arithmetic reconciles:

- **Timesheets:** 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8% per hour.
- **System logs:** 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5%.
- **Halden continuers:** 96.8/0.866 gives +11.8%, with hours falling from 40.3 to 34.9 (−13.4%).
- **Mediation:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100%.
- **Meetings:** the treated-minus-control gap is about 3.3 hours at both month 6 and month 24.

The problems are below, roughly in order of importance.

## 1. The control offices changed their own practice

In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their own meetings, and their output per hour rose 4.1%. This is contamination of the control group, not just an interesting side observation. It raises the control mean by roughly 1.2 points (4.1% × 2/7), which shrinks the treated-minus-control estimate.

So part of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may come from **control offices improving**, not treated offices fading. The paper presents the decline as evidence of fading and the meeting audit as a separate curiosity. It should report the 24-month estimate with and without those two offices.

## 2. The headline decline mixes two hours measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data". But 12.5% is a timesheet figure. Logs weren't collected at nine months.

- **Like-for-like (timesheets):** 12.5% to 9.8%, a relative fall of about 22%.
- **The Summary's comparison:** 12.5% to 8.5%, a relative fall of about 32%.

The body handles this correctly. The Summary and Section 5 ("declined by about a quarter") blur the distinction.

## 3. The mediation test is not an independent replication

- **It uses the same seven offices.** The meetings hypothesis came from the treated case-processing offices, and it was tested again on those same offices, using overlapping months, with the model registered at month 11 after the exploratory result was known. Registering the analysis prevents the model from being tuned to the result. It cannot rule out that those particular offices are unusual. Varga & Holm's point that the finding "does not replicate" has been addressed in form but not in substance.
- **Seven treated offices is still very few.** Adding office-months does not add independent units. The interval of 28–66% depends on how standard errors were clustered with 14 offices, and the paper doesn't say.
- **The two mediators are measured with different precision.** Meeting time comes from calendars and is precise. Fatigue comes from a self-report scale and is noisy. Measurement error shrinks the share attributed to the noisier mediator, so the comparison is tilted toward meetings, possibly a lot.
- **There is a confounding problem.** Treatment was randomised, but how much each office cut meetings was not. Better-run offices may both cut meetings and become more productive. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary still says "confirms".

## 4. What do the system logs measure?

The logs record "active log-in time on the case-management system… working on cases". Meetings presumably don't happen on that system. If so, cutting about 3.3 hours of meetings out of roughly 4.5 lost hours means case-work time fell only about 1.2 hours. Log-measured hours would then fall far less than 11%.

That logs (−11%) and timesheets (−12%) fell by similar amounts suggests the logs capture something closer to total hours. This matters for interpreting the mechanism:

- If logs exclude meetings, the meetings pathway means meetings disrupt the case work around them.
- If logs include meetings, it means time was reallocated from meetings to cases.

The authors should define the measure.

## 5. Some questions from nine months remain open

- **Backlog and timeliness are still not reported.** Output per FTE has been 3.4% below control for two years. If arrivals stayed the same, backlog grew by roughly 3.4% of annual volume each year, about 3–4 weeks of work by month 24. Whether statutory deadlines were met was the obvious 24-month question, and it isn't answered.
- **Cost is still not reported** for case-processing, including overtime on top of full pay.
- **The registered primary outcome is output per FTE**, at −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2), with a slightly worse point estimate than at nine months. The Summary leads with the secondary per-hour outcome instead.
- **Sick days** (−27%): it is still not said whether the schedule removed working days, which would make part of the fall mechanical.

## 6. The Halden section

- **Response bias.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded, and reverters are less likely to respond. The 3 of 14 reversion rate is therefore probably an underestimate.
- **The marketing agency doesn't fit the stated category.** The Summary says all reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations". A marketing agency citing client deadlines is discretionary work by the review's coding. Calling it "client-facing" stretches the category to fit the dichotomy. It is better read as evidence that discretionary work with hard external deadlines can also struggle.
- **Two years of uncontrolled change.** Comparing with a pre-pilot baseline more than two years earlier picks up every other change in between, including new tools, process changes and possibly AI adoption in 2024–25. Calling 11.8% an "upper bound" is reasonable as an intuition but it isn't a formal bound.
- **Attrition is still not addressed.** Okafor, an author of the original Halden paper, co-authors this report, which does not respond to Varga & Holm's finding that 7 of the 9 withdrawals came after the schedule started. That correction belongs in the record.

## 7. What is well done

- **The rebuttal of the meta-analysis is decisive.** All four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which confirms the earlier concern that the duration claim was unsupported.
- **The rebuttal of Varga & Holm is fair.** The study meets every standard that re-analysis recommended and still finds a gain whose confidence interval excludes zero. It also concedes what Varga & Holm got right.
- **Ending the counter arm** is informative: waits of 7.3 v 4.0 minutes and 12% more staff needed to restore service. The 12% matches the nine-month per-FTE loss (1/0.886 ≈ 1.13). That a 12% staffing increase raises cost per contact by only 9% presumably reflects non-staff costs, but the basis should be stated.
- **The paper is cautious about reorganisation without an hours cut.** It doesn't claim more than two uncontrolled offices can show, and it correctly notes that no arm tested it.

## Updated picture across the five documents

| Question | Status now |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in discretionary work | Real and moderate: about 8.5–10% at 24 months in the best study, perhaps understated because of contamination |
| Does it fade? | Partly. Down about a fifth like-for-like over 9–24 months, though some of that may be control improvement |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Refuted |
| "No sign of decay" (meta-analysis) | Refuted. Its evidence came from studies with inflated designs |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | Slightly below control (−3.4%, confidence interval includes zero). Backlog consequences unknown |
| Coverage-bound work | Not viable without more staff (about 12% more, raising cost per contact by about 9%) |
| Mechanism | Meetings look important, but the evidence comes from the same 7 offices, is open to confounding, and is tilted against fatigue by measurement error |
| Reorganisation without an hours cut | Untested. It is the obvious next trial: an arm that cuts meetings with no change in hours |

The practical message is stable across the stronger sources. In discretionary work, a cut of about 20% in scheduled hours gives roughly a 12% cut in actual hours. Output per worker is nearly maintained, and the per-hour gain is about 9–10%, which persists for two years at somewhat reduced size. A large part of it may come from removing low-value meetings, which some organisations may be able to do without cutting hours.
